judgments.comparative_verdict: Both reports are strong and comparable on (a)–(c), but Report 1 wins overall by correctly identifying the shared fixed results-DB path as a real concurrent-corruption risk (d), which Report 2 downplays as unused "cheap insurance."

report_1.evidence: `pipeline/registry.py` is named by three findings (F-02, F-05, F-09) and `pipeline/run_batch.py` by four (F-04, F-07, F-13, F-14). Per-finding assignment across different engineers guarantees merge conflicts

report_2.evidence: Engineer C — `pipeline/registry.py`: ... These are three one-line edits in an 11-line file that nothing else imports (verified by grep), so they are trivially safe — but only if one person owns the file.

report_1.evidence: Wave 1 — four parallel batches, one engineer each. ... A — config | F-02, F-05, F-09 | `pipeline/registry.py` ... C — rubric parsing | F-11 (test first), F-01

report_2.evidence: Wave 1 — four parallel streams ... Engineer B — `pipeline/rubric.py`: F-01 ... then F-11 ... Engineer C — `pipeline/registry.py`: F-09 immediately ... then F-02 and F-05

report_1.evidence: F-06 — escalate it, don't assign it. "Thresholds are too lenient; tighten them" is a scoring-policy change, not a bug fix: it changes the score every borderline answer receives ... It needs a decision from whoever owns the rubric/scoring policy

report_2.evidence: F-06 — not an engineering task yet. "Thresholds are too lenient; tighten them" names no target values ... changing it moves every borderline score in future runs and breaks comparability with past results ... An engineer should not pick the numbers; the rubric owner decides

report_1.evidence: `tests/conftest.py:4` points every test run at `RESULTS_DB = /var/tmp/llm-scoring/results.db` unless the `RESULTS_DB` env var overrides it. Multiple engineers running the suite in parallel on the same machine (or CI runner) will stomp the same database file. Each needs a private path.
